Joseph of Arimathea (Doctrinal)
JOH-zef of AR-i-muh-THEE-uh
noun
Greek Iōsēph apo Arimathaias (G2501 + G707) — a wealthy member of the Sanhedrin (Mark 15:43), a secret disciple of Jesus "for fear of the Jews" (John 19:38), who courageously went to Pilate after the crucifixion to ask for the body of Christ and buried Him in his own new tomb.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

📖 Biblical Definition

Joseph of Arimathea is the secret disciple who became a public one at the worst possible moment — when association with Christ meant certain reputational ruin and likely persecution. All four Gospels record him (Matt 27:57-60; Mark 15:43-46; Luke 23:50-53; John 19:38-42). Mark calls him "an honorable counsellor, which also waited for the kingdom of God," and adds that he "went in boldly unto Pilate, and craved the body of Jesus." Luke notes he was "a good man, and a just," and had "not consented to the counsel and deed of them" who condemned Christ. John tells us he was a disciple of Jesus "secretly for fear of the Jews" — until the cross changed him. The wealth that enabled him to own a new rock-cut tomb in a garden (Matt 27:60) is the same wealth that fulfilled Isaiah 53:9 to the letter — "and he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death." Christ was crucified between two thieves (the wicked) and buried in the tomb of a rich man (the rich) — and Joseph's quiet wealth, providentially preserved, fulfilled the prophecy. The lesson is profound: secret discipleship is often broken open by suffering or crisis — the cross outed Joseph as a follower of Christ when comfort and safety had let him stay hidden. Many believers today resemble pre-cross Joseph: silent because of fear, hidden because of cost. The cross calls every disciple out of hiding. Joseph also pictures the gospel reach beyond the working class — Christ saves the wealthy and the powerful, including members of the very Sanhedrin that crucified Him.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A wealthy member of the Sanhedrin, secret disciple of Jesus, who courageously asked Pilate for Christ's body and buried Him in his own new tomb — fulfilling Isaiah 53:9.

expand to see more

JOSEPH OF ARIMATHEA, noun. A wealthy member of the Sanhedrin, secret disciple of Jesus "for fear of the Jews" (John 19:38), who after the crucifixion went boldly to Pilate to ask for the body of Christ and buried Him in his own new rock-cut tomb in a garden (Matt 27:57-60).

All four Gospels mention him: Matt 27:57-60; Mark 15:43-46; Luke 23:50-53; John 19:38-42. His wealth fulfilled Isaiah 53:9 ("with the rich in his death").

📖 Key Scripture

Matthew 27:57-60 — "When the even was come, there came a rich man of Arimathaea, named Joseph, who also himself was Jesus' disciple: He went to Pilate, and begged the body of Jesus. Then Pilate commanded the body to be delivered. And when Joseph had taken the body, he wrapped it in a clean linen cloth, And laid it in his own new tomb, which he had hewn out in the rock."

John 19:38 — "And after this Joseph of Arimathaea, being a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, besought Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus: and Pilate gave him leave."

Mark 15:43 — "Joseph of Arimathaea, an honourable counsellor, which also waited for the kingdom of God, came, and went in boldly unto Pilate, and craved the body of Jesus."

Isaiah 53:9 — "And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death; because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Joseph of Arimathea is corrupted when his late-emerging discipleship is held against him ("why was he hidden until then?"), or when medieval legends (the Grail legend, Joseph in Britain at Glastonbury) eclipse the canonical text.

expand to see more

Hidden-disciple criticism. Some preachers fault Joseph for being a "secret disciple" until the cross — as if his fear before disqualified him from honor after. But the canonical text does the opposite: Joseph's hiddenness BEFORE makes his boldness AFTER more remarkable. The cross outed him when comfort had let him stay invisible. Many believers today face the same arc — silent in comfortable seasons, called out in seasons of crisis. The cross of Christ has a way of breaking open hidden discipleship.

Grail-legend mythologizing. Medieval legend made Joseph the bearer of the Holy Grail to Britain, the founder of Glastonbury Abbey, the great-uncle of Christ, and other accreted myths. None of this is in the canonical text. The historical Joseph was a wealthy member of the Jerusalem Sanhedrin whose only documented action is taking custody of Christ's body and burying Him. The mythologization actually shrinks rather than enlarges his canonical glory — the real Joseph stood up at the worst moment in Israel's history and gave his own tomb to the body of the Messiah.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek Iōsēph apo Arimathaias (G2501 + G707) — Joseph from Arimathea; wealthy Sanhedrin member, secret-then-public disciple.

expand to see more

Greek Iōsēph (G2501) — Joseph; same name as the patriarch and as Mary's husband; a common Hebrew name

Greek Arimathaia (G707) — Arimathea; a town in Judea, possibly Ramah or Ramathaim-Zophim (Samuel's birthplace)

Member of the Sanhedrin (Mark 15:43 "honorable counsellor") who did not consent to Christ's condemnation (Luke 23:51)

Fulfilled Isaiah 53:9 ("with the rich in his death") by providing his own new rock-cut tomb

Usage

"Joseph of Arimathea was a secret disciple until the cross — and at the worst moment for safety, he stood up."

"The wealth Joseph had quietly accumulated fulfilled the prophet's word: Christ was buried with the rich, exactly as Isaiah said."

"Hidden discipleship is often broken open by crisis; comfort lets us stay invisible, but the cross calls us out."
